q: Is there a sharper failure-probability bound than the paper's Lemma 6.3 P(fail) <= 2^{-i/4} for the class of already-balanced hidden subgroups H, closer to the abelian rate 2^{-i}? Our empirical curve at n=2 sits ~10-20 percentage points above the Lemma 6.3 bound at small i, suggesting the analysis is not tight for that subclass.
basis: The stress-sweep table in results/stress_results.json shows empirical success at i=6 samples equal to 0.43-0.90 across five subgroups, versus the paper's worst-case bound 0.646. The gap is consistent across seeds and subgroup types.
next_steps: Repeat the sweep at n=3 and n=4 for 50+ balanced subgroups per class; fit a two-parameter exponential 1 - c * r^i to the empirical curve; try to prove a matching tail bound conditioned on U being balanced.

q: The paper factors the algorithm as (abelian HSP on N) + (non-abelian Fourier sampling for U ∩ U^t). Can these two halves be merged into a single sampling loop that reuses each measurement outcome for both parts of the answer, and if so, does the constant in the O(n) total-query bound drop by ~2x?
basis: Our replication naturally observed that many Fourier samples from Algorithm 7.1 also give information about U ∩ N when restricted to the a=0 support, so the abelian HSP subroutine appears partially redundant in simulation.
next_steps: Instrument the sampler to record, per Fourier sample, whether the outcome (a) lies in N and (b) lies in the affine set separating U^perp from (U^t)^perp; compute the mutual information with U ∩ N and U ∩ U^t; propose a merged classical postprocessing step and re-benchmark query count.

q: How does the algorithm degrade under a noisy or promise-violating oracle f that agrees with a true coset function on only a (1 - epsilon) fraction of W_n? The paper assumes exact promise; the algorithm's exactness would appear to make it brittle.
basis: We reproduced p_success = 1.00 in the exact-promise setting for all 6 initial and 5 non-abelian-focused trials. This is 'too clean' to inform noise tolerance, which matters for any physical implementation.
next_steps: Modify sample_once() to flip the query outcome with probability epsilon (or map to a random coset), sweep epsilon ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, and measure the sample count needed to hit p >= 0.9 as a function of epsilon and n.

q: The paper's outlook (Sec. 8) conjectures generalization to arbitrary split extensions Z_2^n ⋊_phi Z_2 beyond the swap action. Which choices of phi preserve the crucial 'half of U^perp lies in N' balance underlying Lemma 6.3, and which break the factor 1/4 in the exponent?
basis: Our closure verifier and pairing implementation both hardcode the swap action tau: (x,y) -> (y,x). Even reading the paper we could not tell whether the argument survives, say, a non-trivial linear phi on Z_2^n.
next_steps: Reimplement mu and DFT parameterized by an arbitrary invertible F_2 matrix phi ∈ GL_n(F_2); enumerate a few (phi, U) pairs and count |U^perp ∩ N|/|U^perp| to see when balance fails; correlate with the algorithm's empirical success rate at fixed sample count.

q: Are there adversarial subgroups H ≤ W_n (as n grows) for which the effective F_2-dimension of <U^perp, (U^t)^perp> is unusually small, so the classical postprocessing needs disproportionately many samples? Our n=2 and n=3 runs saw uniform success at 4n samples, so any adversarial cases must appear only at larger n.
basis: The paper's bound is worst-case in a subgroup-agnostic sense (Lem. 6.3), but our empirical curve suggests the constant depends on the subgroup class (abelian |U|=2 slower to converge than the |U|=8 mixed subgroup in our sweep).
next_steps: Enumerate all subgroups of W_3 (order 128) up to conjugacy; for each, compute dim_{F_2} <U^perp, (U^t)^perp> and run 1000 reps of the full pipeline at i=4n and i=8n; plot success vs. dimension; identify any subgroup where success at 4n falls below 0.5.
